claim: Neuronal excitation imposes a high demand of ATP in neurons.
source: Neuronal excitation imposes a high demand of ATP in neurons.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about neuronal function.

claim: Most of the ATP in neurons derives primarily from pyruvate-mediated oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Most of the ATP derives primarily from pyruvate-mediated oxidative phosphorylation, a process that relies on import of pyruvate into mitochondria occuring exclusively via the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as background information about neuronal energy metabolism.

claim: Pyruvate import into mitochondria occurs exclusively via the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC).
source: Most of the ATP derives primarily from pyruvate-mediated oxidative phosphorylation, a process that relies on import of pyruvate into mitochondria occuring exclusively via the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: MPC1 is an essential subunit of the MPC.
source: we generated a mouse strain carrying a conditional deletion of MPC1, an essential subunit of the MPC, specifically in adult glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by the experimental design.

claim: Mice with MPC1 deletion in adult glutamatergic neurons have decreased levels of oxidative phosphorylation in excitatory neurons.
source: We found that, despite decreased levels of oxidative phosphorylation and decreased mitochondrial membrane potential in these excitatory neurons, mice were normal at rest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mice with MPC1 deletion in adult glutamatergic neurons have decreased mitochondrial membrane potential in excitatory neurons.
source: We found that, despite decreased levels of oxidative phosphorylation and decreased mitochondrial membrane potential in these excitatory neurons, mice were normal at rest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1C and F.

claim: Neuro-MPC1-KO mice were normal at rest.
source: We found that, despite decreased levels of oxidative phosphorylation and decreased mitochondrial membrane potential in these excitatory neurons, mice were normal at rest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Neuro-MPC1-KO mice rapidly developed severe seizures and died in response to mild inhibition of GABA mediated synaptic activity.
source: Surprisingly, in response to mild inhibition of GABA mediated synaptic activity, they rapidly developed severe seizures and died, whereas under similar conditions the behavior of control mice remained unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Control mice behavior remained unchanged under mild inhibition of GABA mediated synaptic activity.
source: Surprisingly, in response to mild inhibition of GABA mediated synaptic activity, they rapidly developed severe seizures and died, whereas under similar conditions the behavior of control mice remained unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Neurons with a deficient MPC were intrinsically hyperexcitable.
source: We report that neurons with a deficient MPC were intrinsically hyperexcitable as a consequence of impaired calcium homeostasis, which reduced M-type potassium channel activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 5A-D.

claim: The hyperexcitability of MPC-deficient neurons is a consequence of impaired calcium homeostasis.
source: We report that neurons with a deficient MPC were intrinsically hyperexcitable as a consequence of impaired calcium homeostasis, which reduced M-type potassium channel activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 6A-G.

claim: Impaired calcium homeostasis in MPC-deficient neurons reduced M-type potassium channel activity.
source: We report that neurons with a deficient MPC were intrinsically hyperexcitable as a consequence of impaired calcium homeostasis, which reduced M-type potassium channel activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 5I-L and calcium chelation experiments in Figure 6P-R.

claim: Provision of ketone bodies restored energy status in MPC-deficient neurons.
source: Provision of ketone bodies restored energy status, calcium homeostasis and M-channel activity and attenuated seizures in animals fed a ketogenic diet.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1D, E.

claim: Provision of ketone bodies restored calcium homeostasis in MPC-deficient neurons.
source: Provision of ketone bodies restored energy status, calcium homeostasis and M-channel activity and attenuated seizures in animals fed a ketogenic diet.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6A, B.

claim: Provision of ketone bodies restored M-channel activity in MPC-deficient neurons.
source: Provision of ketone bodies restored energy status, calcium homeostasis and M-channel activity and attenuated seizures in animals fed a ketogenic diet.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 5G, H, M, N.

claim: Ketone bodies attenuated seizures in neuro-MPC1-KO animals fed a ketogenic diet.
source: Provision of ketone bodies restored energy status, calcium homeostasis and M-channel activity and attenuated seizures in animals fed a ketogenic diet.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Glucose is oxidized through glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation to produce ATP during neuronal activity.
source: During neuronal activity, the energy demand imposed by neuronal excitation is mainly met by glucose, which is oxidized through glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) to produce ATP (Ashrafi and Ryan, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Pyruvate is transported into mitochondria through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC).
source: Oxidation of glucose starts in the cytosol and generates pyruvate, which, in turn, is transported into mitochondria through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) (Bricker et al., 2012; Herzig et al., 2012), where it fuels the TCA cycle and boosts OXPHOS.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Pyruvate fuels the TCA cycle and boosts OXPHOS in mitochondria.
source: Oxidation of glucose starts in the cytosol and generates pyruvate, which, in turn, is transported into mitochondria through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) (Bricker et al., 2012; Herzig et al., 2012), where it fuels the TCA cycle and boosts OXPHOS.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about mitochondrial metabolism.

claim: Pyruvate can be generated in neurons through oxidation of astrocyte-derived lactate by lactate dehydrogenase.
source: In neurons, pyruvate can also be generated through oxidation of astrocyte-derived lactate by the lactate dehydrogenase (Pellerin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Glucose and pyruvate oxidation via the TCA cycle is required for the synthesis of glutamate and GABA.
source: Besides energy production, glucose and pyruvate oxidation via the TCA cycle is also required for the synthesis of essential molecules, including the neurotransmitters glutamate and γ−aminobutyric acid (GABA).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about neurotransmitter synthesis.

claim: ATP production and neurotransmitter release are tightly linked to glucose and pyruvate metabolism.
source: Therefore ATP production and neurotransmitter release are tightly linked to glucose and pyruvate metabolism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a logical inference from the previous statements.

claim: Mutations in GLUT1 result in severe synaptic dysfunction.
source: Accordingly, genetic pathologies linked to impaired glucose or pyruvate oxidation, such as mutations in the glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) (Brockmann et al., 2001), pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) (Ostergaard et al., 2009), MPC (Brivet et al., 2003; Oonthonpan et al., 2019), or complexes of the respiratory chain (Diaz et al., 2011) result in severe synaptic dysfunction (Beck and Yaari, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Mutations in PDH result in severe synaptic dysfunction.
source: Accordingly, genetic pathologies linked to impaired glucose or pyruvate oxidation, such as mutations in the glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) (Brockmann et al., 2001), pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) (Ostergaard et al., 2009), MPC (Brivet et al., 2003; Oonthonpan et al., 2019), or complexes of the respiratory chain (Diaz et al., 2011) result in severe synaptic dysfunction (Beck and Yaari, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Mutations in MPC result in severe synaptic dysfunction.
source: Accordingly, genetic pathologies linked to impaired glucose or pyruvate oxidation, such as mutations in the glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) (Brockmann et al., 2001), pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) (Ostergaard et al., 2009), MPC (Brivet et al., 2003; Oonthonpan et al., 2019), or complexes of the respiratory chain (Diaz et al., 2011) result in severe synaptic dysfunction (Beck and Yaari, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Mutations in complexes of the respiratory chain result in severe synaptic dysfunction.
source: Accordingly, genetic pathologies linked to impaired glucose or pyruvate oxidation, such as mutations in the glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1) (Brockmann et al., 2001), pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) (Ostergaard et al., 2009), MPC (Brivet et al., 2003; Oonthonpan et al., 2019), or complexes of the respiratory chain (Diaz et al., 2011) result in severe synaptic dysfunction (Beck and Yaari, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Diseases linked to impaired glucose or pyruvate oxidation are associated with brain hypoactivity.
source: Not surprisingly, these diseases are associated with brain hypoactivity, although paradoxically they can be accompanied by neuronal hyperexcitability and behavioral seizures of varying severity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation about these diseases.

claim: Diseases linked to impaired glucose or pyruvate oxidation can be accompanied by neuronal hyperexcitability and behavioral seizures.
source: Not surprisingly, these diseases are associated with brain hypoactivity, although paradoxically they can be accompanied by neuronal hyperexcitability and behavioral seizures of varying severity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a paradoxical observation about these diseases.

claim: The MPC is a heterodimer composed of two subunits, MPC1 and MPC2.
source: The MPC is a heterodimer composed of two subunits, MPC1 and MPC2, inserted into the inner mitochondrial membrane (Bricker et al., 2012; Herzig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The MPC is inserted into the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: The MPC is a heterodimer composed of two subunits, MPC1 and MPC2, inserted into the inner mitochondrial membrane (Bricker et al., 2012; Herzig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Deletion of MPC1 and MPC2 was sufficient to inactivate the carrier activity.
source: Deletion of MPC1 and MPC2 was sufficient to inactivate the carrier activity and its constitutive inactivation in the mouse caused embryonic lethality at E12 (Vanderperre et al., 2016; Vigueira et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Constitutive inactivation of MPC in the mouse caused embryonic lethality at E12.
source: Deletion of MPC1 and MPC2 was sufficient to inactivate the carrier activity and its constitutive inactivation in the mouse caused embryonic lethality at E12 (Vanderperre et al., 2016; Vigueira et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Providing ketone bodies to pregnant females allowed MPC-deficient embryos to survive until birth.
source: Interestingly, providing ketone bodies, which directly feed the TCA cycle with acetyl-CoA and boost OXPHOS, to the pregnant females allowed the embryos to survive until birth (Vanderperre et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Ketone bodies directly feed the TCA cycle with acetyl-CoA and boost OXPHOS.
source: Interestingly, providing ketone bodies, which directly feed the TCA cycle with acetyl-CoA and boost OXPHOS, to the pregnant females allowed the embryos to survive until birth (Vanderperre et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about ketone body metabolism.

claim: Expression of shMPC1_1 or shMPC1_2 produced a significant reduction in MPC1 and MPC2 protein levels.
source: Expression of either of the two shRNAs produced a significant reduction in MPC1 and MPC2 protein levels (the latter being unstable in the absence of MPC1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: MPC2 is unstable in the absence of MPC1.
source: Expression of either of the two shRNAs produced a significant reduction in MPC1 and MPC2 protein levels (the latter being unstable in the absence of MPC1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an explanation for the observed reduction in MPC2 levels.

claim: Genetic and pharmacological impairment of MPC activity resulted in decreased pyruvate-driven basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates.
source: Both genetic and pharmacological impairment of MPC activity resulted in decreased pyruvate-driven basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates (OCR) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and decreased mitochondrial ATP production (Figure 1B), which is consistent with previously published results (Divakaruni et al., 2017; Grenell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Genetic and pharmacological impairment of MPC activity resulted in decreased mitochondrial ATP production.
source: Both genetic and pharmacological impairment of MPC activity resulted in decreased pyruvate-driven basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates (OCR) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and decreased mitochondrial ATP production (Figure 1B), which is consistent with previously published results (Divakaruni et al., 2017; Grenell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ATP measurement data in Figure 1B.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential was significantly reduced in MPC-deficient neurons.
source: Furthermore, mitochondrial membrane potential, measured using mitotracker and TMRE was significantly reduced in MPC-deficient neurons (Figure 1C , F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging data in Figure 1C and F.

claim: MPC-deficient neurons showed increased extracellular acidification rate.
source: This was associated with an increased extracellular acidification rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) and increased glucose uptake, which was measured using the 2-NBDG import assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), two hallmarks of aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: MPC-deficient neurons showed increased glucose uptake.
source: This was associated with an increased extracellular acidification rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) and increased glucose uptake, which was measured using the 2-NBDG import assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), two hallmarks of aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by 2-NBDG uptake data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Increased extracellular acidification rate and increased glucose uptake are hallmarks of aerobic glycolysis.
source: This was associated with an increased extracellular acidification rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) and increased glucose uptake, which was measured using the 2-NBDG import assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), two hallmarks of aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the results as established knowledge about aerobic glycolysis.

claim: Addition of β-hydroxybutyrate rescued oxygen consumption in MPC-deficient neurons.
source: Consistent with this, we found here that addition of the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (βHB) (10 mM) to the culture medium rescued all observed defective functionalities in MPC-deficient neurons, including oxygen consumption, ATP production, membrane potential (Figure 1D-F) and both extracellular acidification rate and glucose uptake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 1D.

claim: Addition of β-hydroxybutyrate rescued ATP production in MPC-deficient neurons.
source: Consistent with this, we found here that addition of the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (βHB) (10 mM) to the culture medium rescued all observed defective functionalities in MPC-deficient neurons, including oxygen consumption, ATP production, membrane potential (Figure 1D-F) and both extracellular acidification rate and glucose uptake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ATP measurement data in Figure 1E.

claim: Addition of β-hydroxybutyrate rescued membrane potential in MPC-deficient neurons.
source: Consistent with this, we found here that addition of the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (βHB) (10 mM) to the culture medium rescued all observed defective functionalities in MPC-deficient neurons, including oxygen consumption, ATP production, membrane potential (Figure 1D-F) and both extracellular acidification rate and glucose uptake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TMRE imaging data in Figure 1F.

claim: Addition of β-hydroxybutyrate rescued extracellular acidification rate in MPC-deficient neurons.
source: Consistent with this, we found here that addition of the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (βHB) (10 mM) to the culture medium rescued all observed defective functionalities in MPC-deficient neurons, including oxygen consumption, ATP production, membrane potential (Figure 1D-F) and both extracellular acidification rate and glucose uptake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Addition of β-hydroxybutyrate rescued glucose uptake in MPC-deficient neurons.
source: Consistent with this, we found here that addition of the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (βHB) (10 mM) to the culture medium rescued all observed defective functionalities in MPC-deficient neurons, including oxygen consumption, ATP production, membrane potential (Figure 1D-F) and both extracellular acidification rate and glucose uptake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by 2-NBDG uptake data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: MPC-deficient neurons display low pyruvate-mediated oxidative phosphorylation and high aerobic glycolysis.
source: Thus, we conclude that MPC-deficient neurons display low pyruvate-mediated oxidative phosphorylation and high aerobic glycolysis, both reversed with βHB.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Induction of Cre activity by injection of Tamoxifen for five consecutive days resulted in deletion of MPC1 FLOXed alleles in the CamKIIα-expressing adult neurons.
source: Induction of Cre activity by injection of Tamoxifen for five consecutive days resulted in deletion of MPC1 FLOXed alleles in the CamKIIα-expressing adult neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: In situ immunofluorescence analyses showed a decrease in neuronal MPC1 immunostaining in various layers of the cortex of neuro-MPC1-KO mice.
source: In situ immunofluorescence analyses showed a decrease in neuronal MPC1 immunostaining in various layers of the cortex of neuro-MPC1-KO mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 2B.

claim: Western blot analysis showed a significant decrease of both MPC1 and MPC2 in neuro-MPC1-KO mice compared to neuro-MPC1-WT mice.
source: Western blot analysis of whole cortex, synaptosomes and mitochondria showed a significant decrease of both MPC1 and MPC2 in neuro-MPC1-KO mice compared to neuro-MPC1-WT mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 2C.

claim: Synaptosomes prepared from the cortex of neuro-MPC1-KO mice displayed lower oxygen consumption compared to synaptosomes from neuro-MPC1-WT mice.
source: Consistent with the results obtained in cultured neurons, we found that synaptosomes prepared from the cortex of neuro-MPC1-KO mice displayed lower oxygen consumption and imported higher amounts of glucose compared to synaptosomes from neuro-MPC1-WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Synaptosomes prepared from the cortex of neuro-MPC1-KO mice imported higher amounts of glucose compared to synaptosomes from neuro-MPC1-WT mice.
source: Consistent with the results obtained in cultured neurons, we found that synaptosomes prepared from the cortex of neuro-MPC1-KO mice displayed lower oxygen consumption and imported higher amounts of glucose compared to synaptosomes from neuro-MPC1-WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by 2-NBDG uptake data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The lack of MPC1 did not affect neuronal cell survival.
source: Importantly, the lack of MPC1 did not affect the neuronal cell survival quantified either by counting the total number of cells, or by the number of apoptotic (TUNEL positive) cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by cell counting and TUNEL assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: At adulthood, both neuro-MPC1-WT and neuro-MPC1-KO genotypes displayed similar body weight and fat mass composition.
source: At adulthood, both genotypes displayed similar body weight and fat mass composition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by body composition data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Adult neuro-MPC1-KO mice showed a tendency toward lower anxiety-like behaviors.
source: At the behavioral level, adult neuro-MPC1-KO mice showed a tendency toward lower anxiety-like behaviors, but no difference in general locomotion, sociability or stress-coping behaviors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Adult neuro-MPC1-KO mice showed no difference in general locomotion, sociability or stress-coping behaviors compared to controls.
source: At the behavioral level, adult neuro-MPC1-KO mice showed a tendency toward lower anxiety-like behaviors, but no difference in general locomotion, sociability or stress-coping behaviors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: All neuro-MPC1-KO mice developed severe, prolonged seizures within 10 min of the first PTZ injection.
source: In contrast, all neuro-MPC1-KO mice developed severe, prolonged seizures (score 6) within 10 min of the first PTZ injection (Figure 3B) and all died during seizures within the next three PTZ injections (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by seizure scoring data in Figure 3B.

claim: All neuro-MPC1-KO mice died during seizures within the next three PTZ injections.
source: In contrast, all neuro-MPC1-KO mice developed severe, prolonged seizures (score 6) within 10 min of the first PTZ injection (Figure 3B) and all died during seizures within the next three PTZ injections (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by survival data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neuro-MPC1-KO mice showed hypersensitivity to kainic acid.
source: When mice were injected with 20 mg/kg kainic acid intraperitoneally, a similar hypersensitivity (score 6) was observed in neuro-MPC1-KO mice indicating that this sensitivity was not restricted to PTZ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by seizure scoring data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The hypersensitivity to pro-convulsant drugs in neuro-MPC1-KO mice was not restricted to PTZ.
source: When mice were injected with 20 mg/kg kainic acid intraperitoneally, a similar hypersensitivity (score 6) was observed in neuro-MPC1-KO mice indicating that this sensitivity was not restricted to PTZ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the kainic acid experiment.

claim: Astro-MPC1-KO mice showed the same response as control animals following PTZ injection.
source: In contrast to neuro-MPC1-KO mice, astro-MPC1-KO mice showed the same response as control animals following PTZ injection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-G), indicating that the phenotype observed in neuro-MPC1-KO mice is linked to the deletion of MPC1 in excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by seizure scoring data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: The phenotype observed in neuro-MPC1-KO mice is linked to the deletion of MPC1 in excitatory neurons.
source: In contrast to neuro-MPC1-KO mice, astro-MPC1-KO mice showed the same response as control animals following PTZ injection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-G), indicating that the phenotype observed in neuro-MPC1-KO mice is linked to the deletion of MPC1 in excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the astro-MPC1-KO experiment.

claim: In neuro-MPC1-KO mice, rhythmic EEG patterns emerged within 5–10 min after PTZ injection.
source: In neuro-MPC1-KO mice, rhythmic EEG patterns emerged within 5–10 min after PTZ injection, invading all electrodes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by EEG recordings in Figure 3C.

claim: The electrical patterns in neuro-MPC1-KO mice coincided with the occurrence of behavioral manifestations of seizures.
source: These electrical patterns coincided with the occurrence of behavioral manifestations of seizures, that is tonic-clonic movements.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the EEG recordings.

claim: Large spike and wave discharges developed in neuro-MPC1-KO mice after PTZ injection.
source: Rapidly thereafter, large spike and wave discharges developed, again invading all surface electrodes and coinciding with numerous fast ripples (Figure 3C, inset).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by EEG recordings in Figure 3C.

claim: The EEG patterns observed in neuro-MPC1-KO mice are characteristic of seizure episodes in humans.
source: Such EEG patterns are characteristic of seizure episodes in humans and were not observed in the PTZ-injected neuro-MPC1-WT mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the EEG data.

claim: The EEG patterns observed in neuro-MPC1-KO mice were not observed in the PTZ-injected neuro-MPC1-WT mice.
source: Such EEG patterns are characteristic of seizure episodes in humans and were not observed in the PTZ-injected neuro-MPC1-WT mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the EEG recordings.

claim: Neuro-MPC1-KO mice develop an epilepsy-like phenotype following administration of a single sub-convulsant dose of PTZ.
source: These data indicate that neuro-MPC1-KO mice develop an epilepsy-like phenotype following administration of a single sub-convulsant dose of PTZ.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the EEG and behavioral data.

claim: The frequency of calcium events in MPC1-deficient neurons was significantly higher than in MPC1-WT neurons.
source: although, interestingly, the frequency of calcium events, as well as the number of co-activation events (i.e. neuronal synchronizations above chance levels) generated in MPC1-deficient neurons were significantly higher than those generated in MPC1-WT neurons (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3F.

claim: The number of co-activation events in MPC1-deficient neurons was significantly higher than in MPC1-WT neurons.
source: although, interestingly, the frequency of calcium events, as well as the number of co-activation events (i.e. neuronal synchronizations above chance levels) generated in MPC1-deficient neurons were significantly higher than those generated in MPC1-WT neurons (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3G.

claim: Neither the amplitude nor the duration of the calcium discharges was modified in MPC1-deficient neurons.
source: In contrast, neither the amplitude nor the duration of the discharges was modified (Figure 3H, I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3H, I.

claim: Neuro-MPC1-KO neurons are more active and are more often recruited into synchronized patterns associated with epileptic activity.
source: These results suggest that neuro-MPC1-KO neurons are more active and are more often recruited into synchronized patterns associated with the epileptic activity.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the calcium imaging data.

claim: The ketogenic diet produces a decrease in glycaemia and an increase in the blood level of β-hydroxy-butyrate.
source: As previously reported (Wirrell et al., 2018), we found that the KD produces a decrease in glycaemia and an increase in the blood level of 3-β-hydroxy-butyrate (βHB), one of the three major ketone bodies generated by the liver (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation and supported by blood measurement data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Mice fed on the ketogenic diet for 1 week were completely resistant to PTZ injection.
source: In addition, we found that mice fed on the KD for 1 week were completely resistant to PTZ injection (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by seizure scoring data in Figure 4A.

claim: Supplementing the drinking water with 1% βHB was sufficient to prevent PTZ-induced seizures.
source: Supplementing the drinking water with 1% βHB was sufficient to prevent PTZ-induced seizures (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by seizure scoring data in Figure 4B.

claim: Intraperitoneal administration of βHB 15 min before PTZ injection significantly reduced the PTZ-induced clinical score of neuro-MPC1-KO mice.
source: Similarly, ip administration of βHB (1 g/Kg) 15 min before PTZ injection, or starvation overnight, both of which conditions led to increased βHB blood levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E), significantly reduced the PTZ-induced clinical score of neuro-MPC1-KO mice (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by seizure scoring data in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Starvation overnight significantly reduced the PTZ-induced clinical score of neuro-MPC1-KO mice.
source: Similarly, ip administration of βHB (1 g/Kg) 15 min before PTZ injection, or starvation overnight, both of which conditions led to increased βHB blood levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E), significantly reduced the PTZ-induced clinical score of neuro-MPC1-KO mice (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by seizure scoring data in Figure 4B.

claim: Supplementing the drinking water with 1% acetoacetate reduced PTZ-induced seizures in neuro-MPC1-KO mice.
source: Similarly, supplementing the drinking water with 1% acetoacetate, another type of ketone body, reduced PTZ-induced seizures in neuro-MPC1-mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by seizure scoring data in Figure 4D.

claim: The phenotype displayed by the neuro-MPC1-KO mice is mainly metabolic in origin.
source: These results indicate that the phenotype displayed by the neuro-MPC1-KO mice is mainly metabolic in origin and is unlikely to be the consequence of neuronal network remodeling.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the ketogenic diet experiments.

claim: The phenotype displayed by the neuro-MPC1-KO mice is unlikely to be the consequence of neuronal network remodeling.
source: These results indicate that the phenotype displayed by the neuro-MPC1-KO mice is mainly metabolic in origin and is unlikely to be the consequence of neuronal network remodeling.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the ketogenic diet experiments.

claim: CA1 pyramidal cells from neuro-MPC1-KO mice exhibited higher discharge frequency compared to neurons from neuro-MPC1-WT mice.
source: CA1 pyramidal cells from neuro-MPC1-KO mice exhibited higher discharge frequency compared to neurons from neuro-MPC1-WT mice when firing was elicited by somatic injections of current ramps of increasing amplitude (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Neurons from neuro-MPC1-KO mice required less current injection to reach the firing threshold.
source: Neurons from neuro-MPC1-KO mice required less current injection (rheobase, Figure 5C) to reach the firing threshold, which was more hyperpolarized when compared to neuro-MPC1-WT cells (Figure 5D).
